title: Unit 9: Macro Economics II
subtitle: Policy, trade, and the wider world

questions.prompt: What is the Federal Reserve (the 'Fed')?
choices: The central bank of the United States
A regular bank where you open a checking account
The agency that collects your taxes
questions.explanation: The Fed is the U.S. central bank. It manages the nation's money and steers interest rates rather than serving everyday customers.

questions.prompt: The Fed's 'dual mandate' is to pursue which TWO goals?
choices: Higher stock prices and more exports
A balanced budget and free trade
questions.explanation: Congress gave the Fed two jobs: keep as many people employed as possible while keeping prices (inflation) stable.

questions.prompt: The Federal Reserve is often called the 'central bank' of the United States.
questions.explanation: A central bank manages a nation's currency and interest rates, and the Fed is exactly that for the U.S.

questions.prompt: The main interest rate the Fed targets is the...
questions.explanation: The federal funds rate is what banks charge each other for overnight loans. When the Fed moves it, other rates across the economy tend to follow.

questions.prompt: Which of these are part of the Fed's job? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Trying to keep inflation low and stable
Setting the income tax rates you pay
questions.explanation: Interest rates, stable prices, and employment are the Fed's turf. Setting taxes belongs to Congress, not the Fed.

questions.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: The institution that manages a nation's money and interest rates
The Fed's twin goals of stable prices and max employment
The key overnight rate the Fed targets
A general rise in prices over time
questions.explanation: These four ideas are the backbone of how the Fed operates and why it exists.

questions.prompt: The Federal Reserve sets the income tax rates that citizens pay each year.
questions.explanation: Taxes are set by Congress (that's fiscal policy). The Fed handles monetary policy, like interest rates.

questions.prompt: When the economy is overheating and inflation is high, what does the Fed usually do?
choices: Raise interest rates to cool it down
Cut interest rates to speed it up
questions.explanation: Higher rates make borrowing pricier, which cools spending and demand, helping bring inflation back down.

questions.prompt: When the Fed LOWERS interest rates, borrowing money generally becomes...
questions.explanation: Lower rates mean cheaper loans, so people and businesses tend to borrow, spend, and invest more.

questions.prompt: Put the steps in order for how a Fed rate HIKE cools the economy.
items: The Fed raises its key interest rate
Loans and credit become more expensive
People and businesses borrow and spend less
questions.explanation: A hike raises borrowing costs, which slows spending, which cools demand and inflation. That's the chain reaction.

questions.prompt: Lowering interest rates is often called 'loosening' or 'easing' monetary policy.
questions.explanation: Cutting rates 'loosens' or 'eases' conditions to give the economy more room to grow. Raising them is 'tightening.'

questions.prompt: The Fed raises its target rate from 4.5% to 5.25%. By how many percentage points did it hike?
questions.explanation: 5.25% minus 4.5% is 0.75 points, which traders also call a '75 basis point' hike.

questions.prompt: Higher interest rates tend to do what to stock prices, all else equal?
questions.explanation: Higher rates make borrowing costlier for companies and make safe bonds more attractive, which often weighs on stocks.

questions.prompt: Which of these are goals of RAISING interest rates? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Make borrowing more expensive on purpose
questions.explanation: Hikes are meant to cool demand and tame inflation. They don't fix employment instantly and can even raise unemployment short term.

questions.prompt: Fiscal policy refers to a government's use of...
choices: Spending and taxes to influence the economy
Interest rates set by the central bank
questions.explanation: Fiscal policy is the government's budget toolkit: how much it taxes and how much it spends.

questions.prompt: Sort each tool by who controls it.
questions.explanation: Taxes and spending are fiscal (government); interest rates and money supply are monetary (Fed). Keeping them straight is key.

questions.prompt: A budget deficit happens when a government spends more than it collects in taxes.
questions.explanation: Spend more than you take in and you run a deficit, covering the gap by borrowing.

questions.prompt: A government collects $3 trillion in taxes but spends $4 trillion in a year. What is its deficit? (Answer in trillions.)
questions.explanation: $4 trillion spent minus $3 trillion collected leaves a $1 trillion deficit for the year.

questions.prompt: 'Stimulus' spending is designed to...
choices: Boost economic activity, often during a slowdown
Pay off all national debt instantly
questions.explanation: Stimulus pumps money into the economy (through spending or tax cuts) to lift demand when growth is weak.

questions.prompt: The national debt is the total of all past deficits (minus any surpluses) a government has piled up over time.
questions.explanation: Each year's deficit adds to a running total. That accumulated total is the national debt.

questions.prompt: Which of these are examples of fiscal policy? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Taxes, spending, and stimulus are fiscal. A Fed rate cut is monetary policy, run by the central bank.

questions.prompt: Match each trade term to its meaning.
pairs: Goods and services a country buys from abroad
Goods and services a country sells to other countries
When a country imports more than it exports
How much one currency is worth in another
questions.explanation: Imports come in, exports go out, and the exchange rate is the price tag that links two currencies.

questions.prompt: An 'exchange rate' tells you...
choices: How much one currency is worth in terms of another
The interest rate on a loan
The price of a single stock
questions.explanation: For example, if 1 euro = $1.10, the exchange rate tells you how many dollars one euro buys.

questions.prompt: A 'strong dollar' means the U.S. dollar buys MORE foreign currency than before.
questions.explanation: A strong dollar has extra buying power abroad, so each dollar swaps for more euros, yen, or pounds.

questions.prompt: Sort each person by which situation helps them.
items: A U.S. tourist traveling in Europe
A U.S. company exporting goods abroad
A foreign tourist visiting the U.S.
questions.explanation: A strong dollar makes foreign goods and travel cheaper for Americans. A weak dollar makes U.S. exports and visits cheaper for foreigners.

questions.prompt: If a country exports MORE than it imports, it has a...
questions.explanation: Selling more abroad than you buy is a trade surplus. The reverse is a trade deficit.

questions.prompt: 1 euro = 1.10 U.S. dollars. How many dollars would you need to buy 50 euros?
questions.explanation: 50 euros times $1.10 each equals $55.

questions.prompt: A weaker dollar tends to make American-made exports cheaper and more attractive to foreign buyers.
questions.explanation: When the dollar is weak, foreign buyers can afford more U.S. goods, which can boost exports.

questions.prompt: A recession is best described as...
choices: A significant, widespread decline in economic activity lasting months
A single bad day in the stock market
Any drop in one company's stock
questions.explanation: A recession is a broad, lasting slump across the economy, not just one rough day or one falling stock.

questions.prompt: A common rule of thumb defines a recession as two consecutive quarters of shrinking GDP.
questions.explanation: It's a handy shortcut. The official U.S. call is broader, but 'two down quarters' is the popular rule of thumb.

questions.prompt: Why do news headlines about the economy often feel scarier than reality?
choices: Dramatic, fearful headlines attract more clicks and attention
They are legally required to exaggerate
questions.explanation: Fear and drama grab attention, so headlines lean sensational. Read past them to the actual data before reacting.

questions.prompt: Experts suggest an emergency fund of 3 to 6 months of expenses. If your expenses are $1,500 a month, how much is a 3-month fund?
questions.explanation: 3 months times $1,500 equals $4,500 of cushion.

questions.prompt: Why does an emergency fund matter during a recession? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Job losses are more common, so income can stop
It lets you avoid selling investments at a low point
It covers surprise expenses without new debt
It guarantees the stock market will go up
questions.explanation: A cash cushion buys you time and options when income drops. Nothing, though, guarantees which way markets move.

questions.prompt: Order these calm, smart responses to a scary economic headline.
items: Take a breath instead of panic-selling
Read past the headline to the real numbers
Revisit your long-term plan and goals
Top up your emergency fund if needed
questions.explanation: Pause, check the data, stick to your plan, and shore up your safety net. That beats reacting on emotion.

questions.prompt: Selling all your investments in a panic every time a scary headline appears is a proven path to wealth.
questions.explanation: Panic-selling usually means selling low. Long-term investors who stay the course tend to do far better.

questions.prompt: The Federal Reserve's dual mandate is to pursue...
choices: A strong dollar and more exports
questions.explanation: The Fed's two jobs are keeping prices stable and employment high.

questions.prompt: Monetary policy (interest rates) is run by the Fed, while fiscal policy (spending and taxes) is run by the government.
questions.explanation: The Fed handles rates and the money supply; Congress handles taxes and spending. Two different toolkits.

questions.prompt: To fight high inflation, the Fed will most likely...
questions.explanation: Raising rates cools spending and demand, which helps bring inflation down.

questions.prompt: Match each policy tool to who controls it.
questions.explanation: Rates and the money supply are the Fed's; taxes and stimulus are Congress's.

questions.prompt: A government spends $5 trillion and collects $4.2 trillion in taxes. What is its deficit? (Answer in trillions.)
questions.explanation: $5 trillion minus $4.2 trillion equals a $0.8 trillion deficit.

questions.prompt: Sort each action into fiscal or monetary policy.
questions.explanation: Rates and money supply are monetary; taxes and spending are fiscal.

questions.prompt: A 'weak dollar' tends to help...
questions.explanation: A weak dollar makes U.S. goods cheaper for foreign buyers, which helps exporters.

questions.prompt: 1 U.S. dollar = 0.80 British pounds. How many pounds do you get for $200?
questions.explanation: $200 times 0.80 pounds per dollar equals 160 pounds.

questions.prompt: Which are smart moves when scary economic headlines appear? (Choose all that apply.)
choices: Keep an emergency fund of 3-6 months' expenses
Check the real data behind the headline
questions.explanation: A cushion, real data, and a steady plan beat panic-selling on a headline every time.

questions.prompt: Put these in order: how a Fed rate CUT is meant to heat up a slow economy.
items: The Fed lowers its key interest rate
People and businesses spend and invest more
questions.explanation: A cut lowers borrowing costs, which lifts spending and investment, which revives growth.
